name: Montagnais
confidence_why: Clarke 1982 states that stress in the Sheshatshit (North West River) dialect, as in most Montagnais dialects, is word-final, and MacKenzie 1980's dialect survey independently assigns final stress to every Innu (palatalized n- and l-) community, the only contrary claim being Burgess 2009's remark that Sheshatshiu has non-final accent, which attributes to Innu a rule MacKenzie 1980 gives for the East Cree and Naskapi y-dialects.
sweep_summary: The single works with stress in the title, Cowan 1983 (IJAL 49:64-71, DOI 10.1086/465765), is closed access everywhere checked (Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, publisher 403, JSTOR/HathiTrust blocked) and was not read; from its title and from what Clarke 1982 (p. 31, fn. 21) and MacKenzie 1980 (pp. 47-48) say about the same phenomenon it is about the length/pitch/stress marking of the inanimate plural on the final syllable after apocope, i.e. morphological suprasegmentals rather than default stress placement; medium priority to acquire. The catalog codes mont1268 fixed: final syllable (dominant) on Clarke 1982 p. 8 ('stress in NWRM, as in most other Montagnais dialects of eastern Quebec-Labrador, is word-final'), re-confirmed held by the project. The better language-wide statement, read this search of works with stress in the title, is MacKenzie 1980 sec. 2.2 (pp. 45-49, Map 2-4): word-final stress only in the eastern, French-contact zone; the western dialects have non-final, quantity-sensitive stress (rightmost underlying long vowel, else penult/antepenult). This refines the catalog: keep fixed: final syllable for the eastern dialects, add a variety caution. Newly downloaded Burgess 2009 (MUN MA thesis, p. 32) even places Sheshatshiu among the non-final pitch accent dialects, contradicting Clarke for the same community; MacKenzie's chapters 'The Language of the Montagnais and Naskapi in Labrador' (scanned) and Drapeau/Ford/Noreau-Hebert 1975 are silent. The one dedicated stress study, Ford 1976 'L'accentuation dans le montagnais de la Moisie', is print-only (not in the Carleton OJS run) and is the top acquisition target; Mailhot 1975 (stress diminution under final-vowel loss, p. 39) was not searched. only direct download, automated download and API lookups were used.

new_statements.quote: There are two major patterns of stress for words in the palatalized dialects: final and non-final. The distribution of patterns is shown on Map 2-4. The extent of word-final stress coincides very neatly with the area of French influence. [...] For those dialects in which stress is non-final, it is difficult to formulate a rule of stress assignment. In di-syllables the long vowel again receives the stress, the penultimate one in the case of a word having two long vowels. [...] In words of three syllables or more, stress usually falls on the rightmost underlying long vowel.
new_statements.citation: MacKenzie, Marguerite (1980). Towards a Dialectology of Cree-Montagnais-Naskapi. PhD thesis, University of Toronto, sec. 2.2 'Stress Placement', pp. 45-49.
new_statements.reading: Montagnais (mont1268) is not uniformly word-final: MacKenzie's dialect survey divides the Innu dialects into a word-final-stress zone (eastern: Lower North Shore and Labrador, the FINAL area on Map 2-4, which is where Clarke 1982's NWRM statement sits) and a non-final zone (western Quebec dialects) with quantity-sensitive stress on the rightmost underlying long vowel, otherwise the penult or antepenult. The catalog's fixed: final syllable coding is right for the eastern dialects and wrong as a language-wide statement; the record needs a variety caution (final = eastern dialects incl. Sheshatshiu per Clarke 1982; non-final, weight-sensitive = western dialects per MacKenzie 1980; Burgess 2009 p. 32 disagrees about Sheshatshiu).

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: MacKenzie 1980 CORROBORATES the catalog's word-final coding for mont1268 as a whole rather than splitting it. Her NON-FINAL zone on Map 2-4 is the palatalized y-dialect area (East Cree communities and Fort Chimo Naskapi), not the western Innu dialects: the isogloss runs from the Saguenay/Lac Saint-Jean north to about 55N and then east, and every Montagnais (L) and (N) community in her Figure 1-1 table (Pointe Bleue, Betsiamites, Sept-Iles/Maliotenam, Schefferville, Mingan, Natashquan, La Romaine, St. Augustin, North West River) lies on the FINAL side. Her own rule summary makes this explicit:…

tone_statements.citation: Stevenson, Sophia (2006). The production and comprehension of tone in Innu. Memoire de maitrise en linguistique, Universite du Quebec a Montreal (dir. Lynn Drapeau). Montreal.
tone_statements.quote: Dans le but de fournir des données phonétiques synchroniques, qui permettraient de confirmer l'existence et l'emploi des tons dans le dialecte de l'Ouest, et pour connaître les éléments phonétiques qui jouent dans la production de ce phénomène, nous avons choisi d'effectuer un test de production et un test de compréhension auprès de plusieurs locuteurs natifs de deux communautés innues (Betsiamites et Sept-Iles). Nos résultats démontrent l'existence d'un ton bas sur la syllabe finale des mots qui ont subi le processus d'apocope ou celui de dégemination des consonnes en finale de mot.
tone_statements.translation: In order to provide synchronic phonetic data that would confirm the existence and use of tones in the Western dialect, and to identify the phonetic elements involved in producing this phenomenon, we ran a production test and a comprehension test with several native speakers from two Innu communities (Betsiamites and Sept-Iles). Our results demonstrate the existence of a low tone on the final syllable of words that have undergone apocope or word-final consonant degemination.
tone_statements.locator: resume / abstract, Archipel UQAM record 3239 (thesis body not)
tone_statements.summary: Restricted (marginal) tone contrast in western Innu: word-final syllables carry a low tone when a final short vowel was apocopated or a final geminate degeminated, contrasting with the default final (rising/high) accent; distinguishes lexical and inflectional forms; confirmed by production and perception tests.

tone_statements.citation: Martin, Pierre (1980). Des tons en montagnais? Cahier de linguistique no 10 (Inuktitut et langues amerindiennes du Quebec), 175-194. Montreal: Les Presses de l'Universite du Quebec. DOI 10.7202/800090ar.
tone_statements.quote: Notre recherche tend à montrer que les Montagnais font effectivement une différence entre ces formes verbales. Notre recherche tend également à montrer qu'en l'occurrence ici la hauteur est utilisée à des fins distinctives. ... Les formes ont été correctement identifiées. Ce qui tendrait à confirmer notre hypothèse. Il y aurait donc, au niveau de certaines formes verbales, des tons (montant et descendant) en montagnais. Voici, à titre d'exemple, la transcription phonologique que nous proposons pour les six premiers mots de notre corpus :
tone_statements.translation: Our research tends to show that the Montagnais do indeed make a difference between these verbal forms. Our research also tends to show that in this instance pitch is used for distinctive purposes. ... The forms were correctly identified. Which would tend to confirm our hypothesis. There would thus be, in certain verbal forms, tones (rising and falling) in Montagnais. Here, by way of example, is the phonological transcription we propose for the first six words of our corpus:
tone_statements.locator: p. 194, Conclusion; supporting F0 findings p. 193, Synthèse
tone_statements.summary: Acoustic study (Mingan/Natashquan): pitch distinguishes certain imperative verb forms; tentatively posits rising and falling tones on the final vowel of those forms; main accent generally word-final.

sources.note: Language-wide dialect survey: the palatalized (Montagnais/Innu) dialects split into a word-final-stress zone (Map 2-4 labels the eastern area, Lower North Shore and Labrador, FINAL) and a non-final zone (western dialects, NON FINAL) with quantity-sensitive stress on the rightmost underlying long vowel, else penult/antepenult short vowel; at least three degrees of stress. In dialects with final stress and apocope of final short vowels, Mailhot (1975:39) reports diminished stress intensity; in non-final dialects a stress shift marks the inanimate plural (masinahi:kan 'book' vs masinahi:kan 'boo…

tone.quote: the loss of a final short vowel which is a morphological marker always results in a phonetic ... marker being left somewhere in the word. ... In the n and l dialects described by Mailhot, stress is always final so that the deleted vowel is signaled by one of the following: (a) lengthening of the final vowel, (b) lengthening of the final consonant if it is not a stop, (c) absence of a glottal stop or post-aspiration, (d) diminution of intensity level of stress, or (e) a level tone instead of a rising one. The rules which generate these changes remain to be investigated in depth.

tone.summary: Mentions tone once, after Mailhot 1975: in final-stress Montagnais n/l dialects a dropped final vowel (e.g. plural -a) may be signalled by a level instead of a rising tone; no tone system described.

sources.citation: Structures comparees de l'innu et du francais (2018, revised after the Institut Tshakapesh colloquium, Uashat 2016). innu-aimun.ca / grammar.innu-aimun.ca.
sources.quote: L'accentuation du francais est telle que l'accent tonique tombe toujours sur la derniere voyelle prononcee du mot ou du groupe de mots. En innu (et en anglais) l'accentuation est differente. [Translation: French accentuation is such that the tonic accent always falls on the last pronounced vowel of the word or word group. In Innu (and in English) accentuation is different.]
sources.locator: section on accentuation (p. ~9 of the PDF text)
sources.note: Pedagogical contrast for Quebec Innu speakers learning French: Innu accentuation is said to differ from French final accent, without stating where Innu stress falls. Weak evidence that (Quebec) Innu is not simply word-final; consistent with MacKenzie's non-final western zone.

sources.citation: Burgess, Janet A. (2009). Reduplication and initial change in Sheshatshiu Innu-aimun. MA thesis, Memorial University of Newfoundland.
sources.quote: Another piece of phonological evidence for distinctive vowel length concerns the placement of pitch accent. Regarding dialects with non-final accent (which includes Sheshatshiu Innu-aimun), MacKenzie (1980) states that: In di-syllables the long vowel receives the stress, the penultimate one in the case of a word having two long vowels. [...] In words of three syllables or more, stress usually falls on the rightmost underlying long vowel. ... (p. 48)
sources.note: Classes Sheshatshiu Innu-aimun among the NON-final pitch accent dialects and applies MacKenzie's quantity-sensitive rule to it; this contradicts Clarke 1982 p. 8 (word-final stress in NWRM = Sheshatshiu) and, on my reading of MacKenzie's Map 2-4 (Labrador lies in the FINAL zone), also MacKenzie's own map. Secondary claim in an MA thesis on reduplication; not a first-hand stress study, but it is a second opinion on the same community and should be recorded as a caution.

sources.note: Per Stevenson 2006 abstract, Drapeau (1979) is one of the works that 'rendent compte de ce phenomene [les tons] et de son origine dans le dialecte de l'Ouest' (tone from apocope in western Innu); MacKenzie 1980 p. 94 cites Drapeau 1979 for two degrees of length on final tense vowels in Betsiamites and pp. 16-33 for segmental facts. Likely contains the first description of the apocope-conditioned final tone/length contrast in noun inflection (plural, obviative, locative).
